text: Hi Jen. This is the September plan, in about eight minutes. It's built around one idea: you're the friend who happens to sell real estate, and you're from here. Everything that follows comes from that.

Four words before anything else, so nothing tonight sounds like jargon. A reel is a forty-second video of you talking, filmed on your phone. It's how strangers find you. A carousel is a post people swipe through, seven slides. They save it and send it to a friend. It's how strangers start to trust you. The stamp is the small mark on every post with the neighborhood and the zip. And the file is three one-page guides you send to anyone who writes. That's it. No other terms.

Here's the difference between posting and a system. A post is a billboard. A system is a door. Every post starts with something real happening on your streets this week, never a trend. Every post has one job: one person writes to you. An address, a question, or just hi, I've been meaning to reach out. Every reply is already written, in your voice. And what people write back decides what we make next month.

People don't follow an agent. They follow a person who knows the block. You're from here. You translate the scary parts, so nobody has to feel dumb to follow you. And you protect people. Your own words: I'm here for you. That's my job. I do this to protect you and your best interest. That line ends everything now.

This is the month, not the post. September is written: the building has to qualify, the train down Van Nuys Boulevard, the insurance quote before the offer, and just breathe. Four different subjects, four different kinds of people. October is sketched: sellers, a two million dollar listing in your other voice, a downsizer, and a client's first year in the house. What repeats is your face, the stamp, and the close. The subject never repeats, and neither does who it's for.

section: how a post becomes a conversation
text: How one post becomes a conversation, in six steps. Something real happens. You talk for a minute on a voice memo. We build the reel and the carousel in your look. It goes out with the door open. Someone writes, and you answer from a reply that's already written. Then we listen to what they asked. The only new work for you is the minute you talk.

We count replies, not likes. A like, a fire emoji, a new follower, a view from someone in Ohio: nice. We don't chase it. A message with an address, a question about their building, a we're looking this fall, or a simple hi, I've been meaning to reach out: that's a person. That gets the saved reply, the same evening, from you.

How this turns into clients. Four stages. People who see it. People who write. Real conversations. Closings. The shape is the same as your referral business, pointed at strangers. The numbers on the right are yours to fill in. You already know how many warm conversations become clients. We'll know the rest after the first month. Nothing here is promised, and that's on purpose.

In ninety days, this is what the go-to in the Valley looks like on your grid. A series people collect. A stamp on every post. Your face on the cover, and real Valley places inside. The same close every time, until it's the thing people quote back to you, and nobody wonders whether you have time for them.

Your week is about three hours. One voice memo. One filming sitting for both reels. Reply the same evening, in minutes, from a reply that's already written. And when a post does nothing, nothing happens. It's not a report card. We read the month, not the Tuesday.

The slow weeks are part of the plan. Three closings and a sick kid is most months, and the system is built for that month. There's no streak to protect. The file keeps working without you on camera. A good reel reruns later with a new stamp. And one voice memo restarts everything when you're back. No makeup posts. No guilt.

Who does what. You talk for a minute, film in one sitting, answer the same evening, and say that's not me whenever a line isn't you. We find what's real, write it from your memo, build the look, post it, read every reply, and adjust. Nothing posts you haven't read. Every word is yours before it's anyone's.

When someone writes, this is what you hand them: the Valley file. Three one-page guides in your look. The four things to read before you write. The insurance question before the offer. The eleven p.m. rate note. And a pinned post on your profile that says start here, so a stranger who just watched a reel knows exactly who you help. You send it because they wrote. No form, no catch.

What we need from you. Three phone photos: you on a Van Nuys sidewalk, you at a condo front door, you holding an H O A packet. Your real take on the train, as a voice memo. How many you can film in one sitting. And your three numbers, so the math on board eight is real.

If you say yes, this is how it runs. This week: the photos, the memo, the numbers, and the first post goes out. Every week after: one memo from you, two reels and a carousel from us. Every quarter: a short note to the people who already know you, in your words. And what you never do: post daily, chase trends, say top producer, or write a caption from scratch.
The first post is ready. Reel one: your credit can be perfect, and the condo still falls through. Then the condo carousel, the next day. Then the reply, already written. Here's the carousel.
The cover. You on the front step. The stamp says Van Nuys. And the question under the one a.m. scroll: what if the building is the problem, not me?

Slide two. You were pre-approved. The building wasn't. Since August third, banks check the building's books on almost every regular condo loan. Four things, mapped: the savings account, twelve months of meeting notes, the building's own insurance, and who's behind on dues.
Slide three, the savings account. You open the budget before you look at the balcony. Ten percent of the building's budget set aside today. Fifteen percent for loans dated January fourth or later.

Slide four, the dark one. Somewhere around page four of the meeting notes: roof discussed. That's a surprise bill, split between every owner, and it was in the notes months before it hits the mailbox.
Slide five, the building's own insurance. If your share of one claim goes over fifty thousand dollars, the loan stops. And the policy has to cover a full rebuild. The building's policy, not yours.

Slide six, who's behind on dues. Fifteen percent or more of units sixty days behind, and no bank lends on the building. Yours included. You can pay yours perfectly, every month. It doesn't change the answer.
And the close. Send me the address before you write. We'll read the four documents together and go from there. Then your line, and my DMs are open. The sources sit at the bottom of the slide.

The week after: the train. That torn-up median on Van Nuys Boulevard is a light rail line, and it doesn't open until December twenty thirty-one. Same look, same stamp. The opinion inside is a draft of yours, until you send your own.
Then the insurance quote before the offer, stamped Sherman Oaks. Fully approved, and the quote still moves your payment. Every number is sourced on the last slide.
And the saved reply, for the night the first address arrives. Paste, add their name, send. That's the whole system. Everything works out exactly the way it's supposed to.
